questions.q: Compare the penetrating power and ionising power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation. Which statement is correct?
options: Alpha particles have the highest penetrating power and the lowest ionising power
Alpha particles have a low penetrating power and high ionising power, while gamma rays have very high penetrating power and very low ionising power
Beta particles are stopped by a sheet of paper, while alpha particles pass through many centimetres of lead
Gamma rays are deflected through a magnetic field as if they carry positive charge
questions.explanation: Ionising power is the inverse of penetrating power. Alpha particles interact most strongly with matter, so they have low penetrating power (stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air) but high ionising power; gamma rays are barely affected by air and need centimetres of lead, so they have very high penetrating power but very low ionising power.

questions.q: On the graph of average binding energy per nucleon plotted against mass number, which nucleus is the most stable, and what does this imply for nuclear fusion and fission?
options: Hydrogen-1 is the most stable nucleus, so only fission can release energy
Iron-56 is the most stable nucleus; joining light nuclei (fusion) and splitting heavy nuclei (fission) both produce nuclei with higher average binding energy per nucleon, releasing energy
Uranium-235 is the most stable nucleus, so fusion absorbs energy at every mass number
Helium-4 is the most stable nucleus, so neither fusion nor fission can release energy
questions.explanation: The graph of average binding energy per nucleon shows the most stable nuclei have a mass number of about 50 to 60, and the most stable nucleus is iron-56. Joining light nuclei produces nuclei with a higher average binding energy per nucleon, releasing energy (fusion); splitting a large nucleus also produces nuclei higher on the curve, again releasing energy (fission).

questions.q: The mass of a helium atom is 4.002603 u and the mass defect of the helium nucleus is 0.030377 u. Calculate the total binding energy of the helium nucleus and its average binding energy per nucleon.
questions.given: mass defect = 0.030377 u;  1 u = 931.5 MeV;  helium-4 has 4 nucleons
questions.explanation: Convert the mass defect to energy using the standard factor 1 u = 931.5 MeV to get the total binding energy of 28.30 MeV, then divide by the 4 nucleons in helium-4 to get the average binding energy per nucleon of 7.08 MeV.

questions.q: A radioisotope sample has a half-life of 10.0 minutes. Calculate the time it will take for its activity to drop from 8.0 MBq to 1.0 MBq.
questions.given: half-life \(t_{1/2} = 10.0\) minutes;  activity falls from 8.0 MBq to 1.0 MBq
working: When half the sample has decayed, the activity also halves.
questions.explanation: Halving the activity each half-life means 3 half-lives have passed before the activity is 1.0 MBq, so the time taken is 3 × 10.0 = 30.0 minutes.

questions.q: State the model of half-life in radioactive decay: give the relationship between the number of atoms remaining and time, and the relationship between the decay constant and the half-life.
keyPoints: The rate of decay is proportional to the number of atoms present: dN/dt = −λN, where λ is the decay constant.
Integrating gives Nt = N0 e^(−λt), where N0 is the number of atoms at t = 0 and Nt is the number at time t.
The decay constant and half-life are inversely related: λ = ln(2)/t½ ≈ 0.6931/t½.
questions.explanation: If you recalled the exponential decay law Nt = N0 e^(−λt) and that the decay constant λ equals ln(2) divided by the half-life, mark it Good or Easy. The two are inversely related, so a short half-life means a large decay constant and fast decay.

questions.q: Using the quark model, account for the charges of the proton and the neutron.
options: A proton is two up quarks and one down quark (+2/3 +2/3 −1/3 = +1); a neutron is one up quark and two down quarks (+2/3 −1/3 −1/3 = 0)
A proton is three up quarks (+2); a neutron is three down quarks (−1)
A proton is one up quark and one down quark; a neutron is two up quarks
Both the proton and the neutron are made of a single quark each
questions.explanation: Each up quark carries a charge of +2/3 and each down quark −1/3. A proton is composed of two up quarks and one down quark, giving a charge of +1; a neutron is composed of one up quark and two down quarks, giving a neutral charge of 0.

questions.q: In the Standard Model, which statement about the gauge bosons that carry the fundamental forces is correct?
options: Gluons carry the electromagnetic force and photons carry the strong nuclear force
Photons carry the electromagnetic force, gluons carry the strong nuclear force, and the W and Z bosons carry the weak nuclear force, but no boson has been found that carries gravity
The W and Z bosons carry gravity, while gluons carry the weak nuclear force
A single boson, the Higgs, carries all four fundamental forces
questions.explanation: Gauge bosons carry forces: photons carry the electromagnetic force, gluons hold quarks together and carry the strong nuclear force, and the W and Z bosons are responsible for the weak nuclear force. No boson has been found that carries the gravitational force, so gravity is the one force the Standard Model does not explain.

questions.q: On a Hertzsprung–Russell (H–R) diagram, what are the main sequence stars doing, and where do the giants and white dwarfs lie?
options: Main sequence stars are fusing hydrogen in their cores; giants and supergiants lie above the main sequence, while white dwarfs lie below it
Main sequence stars have stopped all fusion; giants lie below the main sequence and white dwarfs above it
Main sequence stars are fusing iron in their cores; white dwarfs are the most luminous stars on the diagram
Every star on the H–R diagram has the same luminosity and surface temperature
questions.explanation: On an H–R diagram most stars cluster along a diagonal main sequence, fusing hydrogen in their cores like the Sun, from hot and luminous down to cool and dim. Above the main sequence are the very large, bright giants and supergiants; below it is a cluster of hot but dim white dwarfs in which fusion has ceased.

questions.q: Hubble analysed the spectra of distant galaxies. What did he find about their red-shift, and what does it imply about the universe?
options: All galaxies are blue-shifted, implying the universe is contracting
Distant galaxies are all moving away from us, and the further away they are the greater their red-shift, which is evidence that the universe is expanding
The red-shift is the same for every galaxy regardless of its distance
Only nearby galaxies are red-shifted, while distant galaxies show no shift
questions.explanation: Analysis of the spectra from galaxies revealed to Hubble that all distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the further away they are, the greater their red-shift. Because the red-shift increases with distance, it is evidence for the expansion of the universe — a single galaxy's red-shift alone would only show motion.

questions.q: For each atomic model, name the single observation that overturned (or, for Bohr, completed) it: the plum pudding model, the nuclear (planetary) model, and Bohr's model.
keyPoints: Plum pudding: the gold-foil rebounds — a diffuse sphere of positive charge cannot bounce an alpha particle straight back, so the positive charge must be concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus.
Nuclear/planetary model: Maxwell's electromagnetism — an orbiting (accelerating) electron must radiate and spiral in, predicting unstable atoms and a continuous spectrum, neither of which we observe.
Bohr's model: it works only for hydrogen and never explains why the orbits are quantised — de Broglie's standing waves supplied the missing mechanism.
questions.explanation: The most-examined reasoning skill in this module is tying each observation to the conclusion it forces. If you linked all three observations to their conclusions, mark it Good or Easy.

questions.q: In a PET scan, when a positron meets an electron they annihilate. Why are the two gamma photons emitted in almost exactly opposite directions?
options: Because charge must be created, not conserved, in the annihilation
Because the electron-positron pair was almost at rest, so the total momentum must stay near zero — the two photons fly off in opposite directions to conserve momentum
Because one photon carries the mass and the other carries the charge of the pair
Because the two photons repel each other electrically once created
questions.explanation: Annihilation converts the entire mass of the electron-positron pair into energy as two gamma photons, each of 0.511 MeV. Because the pair was nearly at rest, the total momentum is almost zero, so the two photons must travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum — the principle the PET scanner uses to locate the annihilation point.
